## What you hand in, and when

There is **no final exam** in Course II. The term project (40 % of the grade) consists of

| Part | Weight | Due |
|---|:---:|---|
| Proposal (`W08_project_proposal.ipynb`) | 5 % | before Week 9 — done |
| Progress talk and code review | 5 % | Week 15 — done |
| **Final presentation** (including live questions on your code) | **10 %** | in the Week 16 session; slides uploaded **before** the session |
| **Final report and code** | **20 %** | **one week after the Week 16 session** (you can use the feedback from your talk) |

The Week 16 session has no quiz: the presentations come first, the course synthesis (short slides, `W16_lecture.html`) closes the session.

**Submit** (one folder or zip, named `AMPS2_project_<student-ID>`):

1. `project.ipynb` — the Colab notebook that produces **every** number and figure in the report. It must run end to end after *Runtime → Restart session and run all*, with `%%fenicsx -np 2`.
2. `report.qmd` **and** the rendered `report.html` — start from `report_template/report.qmd`. Render it with `W16_render_report.ipynb` on Colab or with a local Quarto installation.
3. `figs/` — the figures used in the report, saved by `project.ipynb`.
4. The presentation slides (PDF or HTML).

## The report

At most **10 pages** in print (about 4 000 words plus figures), in English. Equations, tables and figures instead of prose wherever possible. The template contains every required section; keep the headings.
If you chose a topic A–J, its page in `projects/` lists the **required tasks** and the **verification specific to the topic**: both must appear in the report.

| Section | What must be in it |
|---|---|
| 1 Problem | The application and why it matters for your research; geometry, governing equations, boundary and initial conditions, parameters **with units**, the dimensionless groups (Péclet, Damköhler, Thiele, Rayleigh, slenderness, stiffness ratio, …), the quantity of interest (QoI). |
| 2 Model and weak form | Spaces, essential vs natural conditions, the constitutive model and its internal variables, the residual $F(u;v)$ and the Jacobian (derived, or `ufl.derivative` plus a check). **The reductions you make** (2D, axisymmetric, plane strain, periodic cell, one-way coupling, steady state) and why they are valid for your parameters. |
| 3 Numerical choices | Elements and **why they do not lock** or violate inf-sup (Weeks 1, 7, 8, 11); stabilisation and the Péclet argument (Week 12); time stepping and its stability (Weeks 5, 6, 14); Newton, load or parameter continuation; linear solver and preconditioner; the cost on Colab. Where these choices can fail for your parameter range. |
| 4 Implementation | Structure of the code (one short table: function or cell → purpose), solver options, what the model module contains, what is saved and plotted where. |
| 5 Verification | (a) **Manufactured or exact solution**: the **predicted** rates, a convergence table/plot with **observed** rates on at least 4 meshes, errors measured against the exact expression (Week 15). (b) **The topic's own physical check** (topic page) or, for your own topic, a benchmark or analytical limit **with a citation**, and the deviation in %. (c) A balance or conservation check where the model has one (mass, energy, force, flux). (d) `-np 1` and `-np 2` give the same QoI (except branching 1D meshes, Week 7). |
| 6 Results | The topic's design output and a parameter study; the **mesh (and time-step) uncertainty of every reported value** — observed order, Richardson value or GCI (Week 15), or a table on three meshes. Physical interpretation. |
| 7 LLM workflow | What was generated by an LLM, which errors you found, **how** you found each one (which test failed), and how each component was verified. At least three concrete cases. |
| 8 Limitations | What your model and numerics cannot do; what you would do next. |
| References, AI-usage log | Cited sources (papers, textbooks, benchmark data). The AI-usage log table of the course, completed, and the code-provenance note. |

**Numbers.** Every number in the report must come from a cell of `project.ipynb` that you ran. Put a short tag after each table or figure caption
naming the cell (e.g. *"project.ipynb §5.2"*). Do not round away disagreements: if the observed rate is 1.6 where you predicted 2, say so and explain.

## The code

- One notebook, ordered like the report (model module → §5 verification → §6 results). The model code goes into one `%%writefile /tmp/fnx/<name>.py` module (as in every week of this course); `projkit.py` from Week 15 may be pasted in as a second module.
- `%%fenicsx -np 2` for every simulation; ordinary cells only NumPy and matplotlib. Long runs save their results to `/tmp/fnx/*.npz` or Google Drive; the plotting cells read them.
- Print the converged reason (KSP/SNES) of every solve that a reported number depends on — and, for time stepping or continuation, of **every step**.
- Total run time on Colab: **at most 30 minutes** (Colab was about 4 times slower than a laptop in Week 15). If the full study takes longer, run the expensive part once, save the results, and add a cell with a reduced version (coarser mesh) that reproduces the trend.
- Code you did not write (LLM, demos, tutorials, the course modules) is allowed — and must be listed in the AI-usage log and the code-provenance note.

## The presentation

**12 minutes per student: 8 minutes talk + 4 minutes questions.** Strict timing.

1. Problem, reductions and QoI (1 slide)
2. Model, weak form and the one numerical choice that matters most for your problem (1–2 slides)
3. Verification: the convergence plot with predicted slopes and the topic's physical check (2 slides)
4. Results with their mesh uncertainty (1–2 slides)
5. One LLM error you found, and how (1 slide)

**Live questions on your code.** Have `project.ipynb` open. You will be asked to show where something happens in the code (e.g. where a boundary
condition enters, which line sets the Jacobian, where the QoI is reduced over ranks) and to predict what a small change would do — as in the Week 15 code review.
Being unable to explain your own submitted code counts as not having done that part (syllabus, *Academic Integrity*).

## Checklist before you submit

- [ ] *Restart session and run all* in Colab finishes without an error in any `%%fenicsx` cell (an error there does **not** stop *Run all* — read every output), in at most 30 minutes
- [ ] Every number in `report.html` appears in an output of `project.ipynb`, with a source tag
- [ ] Predicted **and** observed convergence rates on ≥ 4 meshes, errors against the exact expression; the topic's physical check with a deviation in %
- [ ] The mesh uncertainty of every reported result (observed order, Richardson, GCI, or three meshes)
- [ ] `-np 1` and `-np 2` give the same QoI
- [ ] The reductions and the element choice are justified (locking, inf-sup, Péclet)
- [ ] Section 7 (LLM workflow) with at least three concrete cases; AI-usage log and code provenance filled in
- [ ] `report.html` renders with figures embedded (open it on another computer)
